docs.title: GoVEX
docs.text:
Vulnerability management library and CLI toolkit for Go

GoVEX is a comprehensive solution for creating, consolidating, and sharing vulnerability reports across multiple formats including XLSX, CSV, Markdown, JSON, and git repositories.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Generic Vulnerability Structs - Unified format for vulnerability data from various sources
  • Multi-Format Reports - Generate XLSX, CSV, and Markdown reports
  • Vulnerability Website - Create Markdown websites for tracking vulnerabilities across projects
  • CI/CD Integration - Commands with proper exit codes for pipeline integration
  • SLA Management - Track remediation SLAs with severity-based policies
  • Compensating Controls & Residual Risk - Model inherent vs. residual severity and risk, with exception-driven SLA switching
  • Risk Ratings - Likelihood × impact matrices with NIST SP 800-30 scale translation
  • Security Letters - Generate SLA exception and hardening notification letters

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/govex"

// Create a vulnerability set
vulns := govex.Vulnerabilities{
    {
        ID:       "CVE-2024-1234",
        Title:    "SQL Injection in login form",
        Severity: "High",
        Status:   "Open",
    },
}

// Generate a table for reporting
table := vulns.Table(govex.TableColumnDefinitionSetSASTSCAReport())

// Export to XLSX
table.WriteXLSX("vulnerabilities.xlsx")

docs.title: govex report
docs.text: Generate a Markdown, HTML, PDF, or JSON vulnerability report from a GoVEX JSON file. The output format is inferred from the output file extension.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
# HTML report from a vulnerabilities set JSON
govex report -i vulns.json -o report.html

# PDF with metadata and residual columns
govex report -i vulns.json -o report.pdf \
  --title "Q3 Vulnerability Report" \
  --organization "Example Corp" \
  --classification "Confidential" \
  --columns residual

# Markdown from a saved Report JSON (metadata preserved)
govex report -i report.json -o report.md

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
The input JSON may be either:

  • A VulnerabilitiesSet file (as produced by govex merge) — the set name becomes the default title.
  • A Report file (as produced by govex report -o report.json or Report.WriteJSONFile) — stored metadata is preserved and flags override it.

docs.title: Flags
docs.text:
Flag Description -i, --input Input JSON file: VulnerabilitiesSet or Report (required) -o, --output Output file: .md, .html, .pdf, or .json (required) -t, --title Report title (defaults to set name) --subtitle Report subtitle --organization Organization name --author Report author --classification Classification banner, e.g. Confidential --summary Executive summary text --columns Findings columns: default or residual

--columns residual renders the inherent vs. residual assessment columns (Residual Severity, Residual Risk, Exception Status, Compensating Controls) — see Compensating Controls & Residual Risk.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide walks through common GoVEX workflows.

docs.title: Creating Vulnerabilities
docs.text:
package main

import (
    "github.com/grokify/govex"
)

func main() {
    // Create vulnerability records
    vulns := govex.Vulnerabilities{
        {
            ID:          "CVE-2024-1234",
            Title:       "SQL Injection vulnerability",
            Severity:    "High",
            Status:      "Open",
            Module:      "backend-api",
            Description: "User input not sanitized in login endpoint",
        },
        {
            ID:          "CVE-2024-5678",
            Title:       "XSS in comment field",
            Severity:    "Medium",
            Status:      "In Progress",
            Module:      "frontend",
        },
    }

    // Generate a report table
    table := vulns.Table(govex.TableColumnDefinitionSetSASTSCAReport())

    // Export to different formats
    table.WriteXLSX("report.xlsx")
    table.WriteCSV("report.csv")
}

docs.title: CISA KEV Integration
docs.text: Integration with CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: import "github.com/grokify/govex/feeds/cisakev"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The CISA KEV catalog lists vulnerabilities that are actively being exploited in the wild. This integration allows you to:

  • Download the KEV catalog
  • Check if your vulnerabilities appear in KEV
  • Prioritize remediation based on active exploitation

docs.title: Load KEV Catalog
docs.text:
// Load from CISA feed
kev, err := cisakev.LoadFromURL()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

// Or load from local file
kev, err := cisakev.LoadFromFile("kev.json")

docs.title: Check for Known Exploited CVEs
docs.text:
// Check if a CVE is in KEV
isExploited := kev.Contains("CVE-2024-1234")

// Get KEV entry details
entry, found := kev.Get("CVE-2024-1234")
if found {
    fmt.Println("Due date:", entry.DueDate)
    fmt.Println("Vendor:", entry.VendorProject)
}

docs.title: Filter Vulnerabilities by KEV Status
docs.text:
// Get vulnerabilities that are in KEV
exploited := vulns.FilterByKEV(kev)

// Prioritize KEV vulnerabilities
for _, v := range exploited {
    fmt.Printf("URGENT: %s is actively exploited\n", v.ID)
}

docs.title: Convert to GoVEX Format
docs.text:
// Convert entire KEV catalog to vulnerabilities
vulns := kev.ToVulnerabilities()

// Generate report
table := vulns.Table(govex.TableColumnDefinitionSetSASTSCAReport())

// Load your vulnerabilities
vulns, _ := govex.ReadVulnerabilitiesFile("scan-results.json")

// Load KEV
kev, _ := cisakev.LoadFromURL()

// Split by KEV status

docs.title: Core Package (govex)
docs.text: The core govex package provides the fundamental types and functions for vulnerability management.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: import "github.com/grokify/govex"

docs.title: Vulnerability
docs.text:
Represents a single vulnerability finding.

type Vulnerability struct {
    ID          string
    Title       string
    Description string
    Severity    string
    Status      string
    Module      string
    Category    string
    CWE         string
    CVSS        float64
    CVSSVector  string
    DetectedOn  time.Time
    // ... additional fields
}

docs.title: Residual Assessment Fields
docs.text:
A vulnerability also carries its assessment before and after compensating controls:

type Vulnerability struct {
    // ...
    Severity               string                // inherent severity (CVSS base)
    SeverityResidual       string                // residual severity (CVSS environmental)
    SeverityResidualVector string                // environmental vector justifying the residual
    RiskInherent           *risk.Rating          // likelihood × impact without controls
    RiskResidual           *risk.Rating          // likelihood × impact with verified controls
    Controls               []CompensatingControl // controls justifying the residual assessments
    Exception              *ExceptionStatus      // exception approval state
    // ...
}

See Compensating Controls & Residual Risk for the full model.

docs.title: CompensatingControl
docs.text:
A measure that reduces exploitability or impact without remediating the vulnerability:

control := govex.CompensatingControl{
    ID:              "CTRL-NET-001",
    Name:            "Network segmentation",
    Function:        govex.ControlFunctionPreventive, // or Detective, Corrective
    Reduces:         []string{govex.ReducesLikelihood},
    ModifiedMetrics: []string{"MAV:A"},
    Effectiveness:   govex.EffectivenessHigh,
    Verified:        true,
}

docs.title: ExceptionStatus
docs.text:
Approval state of a risk exception. The SLA clock runs on inherent severity until an exception is approved, then on residual severity:

vn.Exception = &govex.ExceptionStatus{
    Status:     govex.ExceptionStatusApproved,
    ApprovedAt: &approvedTime,
    ExpiresAt:  &expiryTime,
}

sev := vn.EffectiveSeverity(time.Now()) // residual while approval in effect

err := vn.ValidateResidualSeverity() // residual must be Critical–Low and ≤ inherent

docs.text:
A slice of Vulnerability with convenience methods.

type Vulnerabilities []Vulnerability

docs.title: VulnerabilitiesSet
docs.text:

type VulnerabilitiesSet struct {
    Name            string

docs.title: Risk Package
docs.text: The risk package provides organization-level risk ratings, explicit risk matrices, and scale translation, including NIST SP 800-30. Risk ratings share the canonical severity vocabulary (Critical, High, Medium, Low) but are derived from a likelihood × impact matrix rather than a CVSS score.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: import "github.com/grokify/govex/risk"

docs.title: Risk Levels
docs.text:
Canonical risk levels, ordered high to low:

Level Notes RiskCritical Shares the severity vocabulary RiskHigh RiskMedium RiskLow RiskNegligible Risk-only floor for residual risk backed by verified controls; no severity counterpart

Informational, None, and Unknown are severity concepts and are not valid risk levels; ParseLevel rejects them.

level, err := risk.ParseLevel("Moderate") // "Medium" — NIST vocabulary accepted as alias
levels := risk.Levels()                   // Critical, High, Medium, Low
all := risk.LevelsWithNegligible()        // + Negligible

docs.title: Ratings
docs.text:
A Rating is a qualitative risk assessment used for both inherent and residual risk:

rating := risk.Rating{
    Likelihood: risk.LevelLow,
    Impact:     risk.LevelHigh,
    Rating:     risk.RiskMedium,
    MatrixID:   "govex-default-4x4",
    Rationale:  "Verified segmentation prevents access from identified threat actors.",
    Confidence: "high",
}

err := rating.Validate()

Inherent risk is assessed as if the relevant compensating controls did not exist; residual risk is assessed given currently implemented, verified controls. See Compensating Controls & Residual Risk.

docs.title: Risk Matrices
docs.text:
The rating for a likelihood × impact combination is an organizational policy choice, not a calculation, so the matrix is an explicit object referenced by ID:

m := risk.MatrixDefault() // common 4×4 matrix

rating, err := m.Rate(risk.LevelLow, risk.LevelCritical) // "High"
err = m.Validate() // every cell must be a canonical risk level

Define your own matrix to encode your organization's policy — for example, whether low likelihood × high impact is Low or Medium:

m := risk.Matrix{
    ID: "acme-3x3",
    Lookup: map[string]map[string]string{
        risk.LevelHigh: {
            risk.LevelLow:  risk.RiskMedium,
            risk.LevelHigh: risk.RiskCritical,
        },
        // ...
    },
}

docs.title: Scales
docs.text:
Ratings are always stored canonically; a Scale relabels them for rendering:

def := risk.ScaleDefault()       // govex canonical vocabulary
nist := risk.ScaleNISTSP80030()  // NIST SP 800-30 vocabulary

label, err := nist.FromCanonical(risk.RiskMedium) // "Moderate"
level, err := nist.ToCanonical("Very High")       // "Critical"

docs.title: NIST SP 800-30 Translation
docs.text:
NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 levels map 1:1 to the canonical scale:

Canonical NIST SP 800-30 Semi-Quantitative Range Representative Value Critical Very High 96 - 100 10 High High 80 - 95 8 Medium Moderate 21 - 79 5 Low Low 5 - 20 2 Negligible Very Low 0 - 4 0

The semi-quantitative values are NIST's published 0-100 assessment scale (SP 800-30 Rev. 1 Appendix G/H/I). They are not CVSS scores; the two must not be conflated.

// Level translation
nist, err := risk.ToNIST80030(risk.RiskCritical)  // "Very High"
level, err := risk.FromNIST80030("Moderate")      // "Medium"

// Semi-quantitative values
v, err := risk.NIST80030ValueFromScore(87)        // High (80-95, representative 8)
v, err = risk.NIST80030ValueFromLevel("Medium")   // Moderate entry; accepts either vocabulary

// Translate a whole rating for FedRAMP-style rendering
out, err := risk.TranslateRatingToNIST80030(rating)
// out.Rating: "Moderate", out.Likelihood: "Low", out.Impact translated;
// rationale, matrix ID, and assessor fields pass through unchanged

Store ratings canonically and translate at the report boundary — TranslateRatingToNIST80030 never mutates its input.

docs.title: Severity Levels
docs.text:
Standard severity levels:

Level Description Critical Immediate action required High Urgent remediation needed Medium Moderate priority Low Lower priority Informational Not a vulnerability; observation or best-practice note (no CVSS score) None Scored vulnerability computing to CVSS 0.0

Informational and None occupy the same reporting tier below Low and are excluded from SLA tracking; they differ in whether a CVSS score exists behind the label. Residual severity (after compensating controls) is restricted to Critical–Low — see Compensating Controls & Residual Risk.

docs.title: Compensating Controls & Residual Risk
docs.text:
GoVEX models the severity of a vulnerability before and after compensating controls, without ever relabeling the original assessment. This preserves the auditable chain:

Finding severity → compensating controls → residual severity / residual risk → exception approval → SLA.

docs.title: The Four Measures
docs.text:
Measure Field Scale Derived From Inherent severity Vulnerability.Severity Critical, High, Medium, Low, Informational, None CVSS base score Residual severity Vulnerability.SeverityResidual Critical, High, Medium, Low CVSS environmental score Inherent risk Vulnerability.RiskInherent Critical, High, Medium, Low (+ Negligible) Likelihood × impact matrix, without controls Residual risk Vulnerability.RiskResidual Critical, High, Medium, Low (+ Negligible) Likelihood × impact matrix, with verified controls

Key distinctions:

  • Severity is technical and recomputable: it comes from a CVSS score with published rating bands. Residual severity is derived from a CVSS environmental vector (SeverityResidualVector) justified by the vulnerability's controls.
  • Risk is an organizational judgment: likelihood × impact looked up in an explicit risk matrix (risk package). It captures what CVSS cannot — asset criticality, data sensitivity, detective controls.
  • The residual risk convinces the exception approver; the approval activates the residual severity; the residual severity drives the SLA.

docs.title: Compensating Controls
docs.text:
A CompensatingControl reduces exploitability or impact without remediating the vulnerability:

control := govex.CompensatingControl{
    ID:              "CTRL-NET-001",
    Name:            "Network segmentation",
    Function:        govex.ControlFunctionPreventive,
    Reduces:         []string{govex.ReducesLikelihood},
    ModifiedMetrics: []string{"MAV:A"}, // CVSS environmental metric this control justifies
    Effectiveness:   govex.EffectivenessHigh,
    Verified:        true,
    VerifiedMethod:  "external-reachability-test",
}

ModifiedMetrics is the load-bearing link: it records which CVSS environmental metric change each control justifies, so the residual severity vector is derived from controls rather than asserted independently.

Detective controls (monitoring, WAF rules) typically modify no CVSS metric — per FIRST guidance, a WAF does not change Modified Attack Vector. Such controls still reduce residual risk and support its Rationale, but should not shrink the SLA-driving residual severity.

docs.title: Exceptions and the SLA Clock
docs.text:
The SLA policy is: the SLA clock runs on inherent severity until an exception is approved, then on residual severity.

vn := govex.Vulnerability{
    Severity:         "High",
    SeverityResidual: "Low",
    Exception: &govex.ExceptionStatus{
        Status:     govex.ExceptionStatusApproved,
        ApprovedAt: &approvedTime,
        ExpiresAt:  &expiryTime,
    },
}

sev := vn.EffectiveSeverity(time.Now()) // "Low" while approval is in effect

EffectiveSeverity returns:

  • Inherent severity when no residual severity is set, no exception exists, or the exception is only requested or rejected.
  • Residual severity while an approved, unexpired exception is in effect.
  • Inherent severity again after the exception expires.

All SLA methods (SLAOverdueDuration, SLACompliant, SLAInfo, BuildSLAStatusString) key off EffectiveSeverity, so an approved exception moves the vulnerability onto the residual severity's SLA timeline automatically.

docs.title: Validation Rules
docs.text:
ValidateResidualSeverity enforces:

  1. Residual severity is Critical–Low only. Informational and None are rejected: Informational is an inherent-only classification for non-vulnerability findings, and "not exploitable" is an exception or VEX status (not_affected), not a severity of None.
  2. Residual can never exceed inherent. Controls cannot make a vulnerability worse; if the environment amplifies it, that is a separate finding.
  3. Absent means absent. An unset residual severity falls back to inherent — do not populate it with Unknown.

docs.title: What Belongs Where
docs.text: GoVEX owns the per-vulnerability record: findings, severities, controls, exceptions, SLAs. Broader risk modeling — assets, attack paths, multi-finding risks, org-level risk registers — belongs in a threat-model layer that references GoVEX findings by ID.

docs.title: SLA Management
docs.text: GoVEX tracks remediation Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with severity-based policies: each severity level gets a number of days to remediate, and every vulnerability's age is evaluated against the policy for its effective severity.

docs.title: SLAPolicy
docs.text:
severity.SLAPolicy defines remediation days for the four actionable severity levels:

import "github.com/grokify/govex/severity"

policy := severity.SLAPolicy{
    CriticalDays: 15,
    HighDays:     30,
    MediumDays:   90,
    LowDays:      180,
}

Informational and None findings are not vulnerabilities requiring remediation and have no SLA days; severities without configured days return 0 and produce no due date via SLAOptions.DueDate.

docs.title: SLAMap and Predefined Policies
docs.text:
severity.SLAMap is a simple severity → days map, with predefined policies for common frameworks:

fedramp := severity.SLAMapFedRAMP() // Critical/High: 30, Medium: 90, Low: 180
gitlab := severity.SLAMapGitLab()   // Critical/High: 30, Medium: 90, Low: 180

docs.title: Policy Methods
docs.text:
// Due date for a severity from a start time
due, err := policy.DueDate("High", detectedTime)

// Overdue check from an age
overdueBy, isOverdue, err := policy.IsOverdue("High", age)

// Days configured for a severity
days := policy.SeveritySLADays("High") // 30

// Render the policy for reports
md := policy.Markdown()
tbl := policy.Table()

docs.title: SLA Statuses
docs.text:
Status strings for reporting:

Constant Value Meaning StatusWithinSLA Within SLA Age is inside the remediation window StatusApproachingSLA Approaching SLA Nearing the SLA threshold StatusOutOfSLA Out of SLA The remediation window has been breached 
status, err := policy.SLAStatusTimesString("High", &startTime, evalTime, "Unknown")
// "Within SLA" or "Out of SLA"; the unknown string when startTime is nil

docs.title: Vulnerability SLA Methods
docs.text:
govex.Vulnerability evaluates its own SLA state against a policy. The SLA clock starts at SLATimeStart:

vn := govex.Vulnerability{
    Severity:     "High",
    SLATimeStart: &detectedTime,
}

overdueBy := vn.SLAOverdueDuration(policy, time.Now()) // 0 if within SLA
compliant := vn.SLACompliant(policy, time.Now())
elapsed := vn.SLAElapsed(policy, time.Now())
ageDays, overdueDays, overdue := vn.SLAInfo(slaMap, time.Now())

// Sets and returns vn.SLAStatus for report columns
status := vn.BuildSLAStatusString(policy, time.Now(), "Unknown")

docs.title: Effective Severity: Exceptions Switch the SLA Basis
docs.text:
All vulnerability SLA methods key off EffectiveSeverity, not the raw Severity field. The policy is:

The SLA clock runs on inherent severity until a risk exception is approved, then on residual severity for as long as the approval is in effect.

vn := govex.Vulnerability{
    Severity:         "High", // inherent: 30-day SLA
    SeverityResidual: "Low",  // residual: 180-day SLA
    SLATimeStart:     &detectedTime,
}

// Before approval: evaluated as High.
vn.SLACompliant(policy, evalTime)

// After approval: evaluated as Low.
vn.Exception = &govex.ExceptionStatus{
    Status:     govex.ExceptionStatusApproved,
    ApprovedAt: &approvedTime,
    ExpiresAt:  &expiryTime,
}
vn.SLACompliant(policy, evalTime)

// After expiry: evaluated as High again.

A residual severity with a merely requested or rejected exception has no effect on the SLA. See Compensating Controls & Residual Risk for the full model.

docs.title: SLA Start Dates
docs.text:
severity.SLAOptions resolves the SLA start time with explicit precedence — a hard per-finding start date, then a fixed program-wide start date, then the finding's soft start date:

opts := severity.SLAOptions{
    SLAStartDateFixed: &programStartDate,
    SLAPolicy:         &policy,
}

due, err := opts.DueDate("High", softStart, hardStart)
// hardStart > SLAStartDateFixed > softStart; nil when no SLA days configured

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Security vulnerability statuses help track the lifecycle of a vulnerability from discovery to resolution. Here are common statuses used in vulnerability management systems:

  1. New/Identified
  2. The vulnerability has been discovered but not yet analyzed or validated.
  3. Examples:
    • A new CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) is reported.
    • An internal system scan detects a potential issue.
  4. Analyzing
  5. The vulnerability is being investigated to determine its validity, impact, and scope.
  6. Security teams assess the exploitability, risk, and affected systems.
  7. Confirmed/Validated
  8. The vulnerability is verified as legitimate and actionable.
  9. Documentation includes details such as CVE identifiers, affected versions, and potential exploit paths.
  10. Mitigated
  11. Temporary measures or workarounds have been applied to reduce the immediate risk (e.g., disabling a vulnerable service or applying a firewall rule).
  12. The issue still requires a permanent fix.
  13. In Progress
  14. Efforts to remediate the vulnerability (e.g., patch development, system updates) are underway.
  15. May include testing fixes in development or staging environments.
  16. Resolved/Fixed
  17. A patch or update has been applied to address the vulnerability permanently.
  18. Verified through testing and audit to confirm effectiveness.
  19. Remediated
  20. All affected systems and environments have been updated or patched, and the risk is eliminated.
  21. Includes a formal review to confirm that remediation was comprehensive.
  22. Closed
  23. The vulnerability is considered resolved, and no further action is required.
  24. Documentation of actions taken is archived for future reference.
  25. Reopened
  26. The issue re-emerges due to failed remediation, additional exploits, or recurrence.
  27. Indicates the need for further investigation or updated fixes.
  28. Not Applicable/False Positive
  29. The vulnerability was misclassified, irrelevant, or not exploitable in the current environment.
  30. Documented as a non-issue with justification.
  31. Deferred/Postponed
  32. Remediation is delayed due to lower priority, resource constraints, or minimal impact.
  33. Often scheduled for future resolution.
  34. Ignored/Accepted Risk
  35. The organization decides not to address the vulnerability based on an acceptable level of risk.
  36. Requires formal approval and documentation of the decision.

docs.title: Workflow Summary
docs.text:
Statuses typically follow a workflow such as:

New → Analyzing → Confirmed → In Progress → Resolved → Closed

or

New → Analyzing → Deferred/Ignored (for non-actionable cases).

docs.title: Vulnerability Reporting Formats
docs.text: This document compares common formats for vulnerability reporting, remediation tracking, and security advisories.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Several standards exist for machine-readable vulnerability information. The choice depends on the use case:

Format Best For Standard Body CycloneDX + VEX Internal triage, CI/CD pipelines, container scans OWASP CSAF Vendor security advisories, CVE publication OASIS/FIRST OSCAL FedRAMP compliance, POA&M tracking NIST SPDX + VEX License compliance with vulnerability context Linux Foundation OpenVEX Lightweight exploitability statements OpenVEX community

docs.title: CycloneDX + VEX
docs.text:
Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX) embedded in CycloneDX SBOMs.

Strengths:

  • Lightweight and CI/CD friendly
  • Native SBOM integration
  • Supports false positive justifications
  • Strong tool ecosystem (Grype, Anchore, Dependency-Track)

Use Cases:

  • Container scan triage (MS Defender, AWS Inspector)
  • Internal vulnerability management
  • DevSecOps pipelines
  • Exploitability context for specific deployments

Tool Support: Grype, Anchore, IntelliJ, VS Code, Dependency-Track

docs.title: CSAF (Common Security Advisory Framework)
docs.text:
OASIS standard for structured security advisories, successor to CVRF.

Strengths:

  • Purpose-built for CVE advisories
  • Rich metadata (CPE, PURL, CVSS, CWE)
  • Supports signed advisories and public feeds
  • Designed for downstream automation

Use Cases:

  • Vendor security bulletins
  • Public CVE disclosure
  • Security advisory aggregation
  • Threat intelligence feeds

Adopters: Red Hat, Cisco, Siemens, SUSE, GitHub

Limitations:

  • Heavyweight for internal triage
  • Not optimized for "is this exploitable in my environment?" workflows
  • Less tight SBOM integration

docs.title: OSCAL (Open Security Controls Assessment Language)
docs.text:
NIST standard for security assessment and compliance documentation.

Strengths:

  • FedRAMP/NIST RMF alignment
  • POA&M (Plan of Action & Milestones) support
  • Structured compliance documentation
  • System Security Plan (SSP) automation

Use Cases:

  • FedRAMP authorization packages
  • NIST 800-53 control assessment
  • Compliance tracking and auditing
  • GRC (Governance, Risk, Compliance) workflows

Limitations:

  • Not designed for CVE-centric reporting
  • Lacks CVSS, exploitability indicators
  • No affected product enumeration (CPE/PURL)
  • Limited use outside regulated compliance

Note: OSCAL POA&M can track vulnerabilities as "weaknesses" but lacks the structured CVE data that CSAF provides.

docs.title: SPDX + VEX
docs.text:
Linux Foundation SBOM standard with VEX extension.

Strengths:

  • Strong foundation for license compliance
  • Linux Foundation backing
  • Growing VEX support

Limitations:

  • VEX extension less mature than CycloneDX
  • Not yet dominant in container vulnerability workflows

docs.title: OpenVEX
docs.text:
Google-backed lightweight VEX format.

Strengths:

  • Simpler than full SBOM+VEX
  • Focused purely on exploitability statements

Limitations:

  • Early adoption phase
  • Limited tool support currently

docs.text: Use Case Recommended Format Container scan triage CycloneDX + VEX CI/CD vulnerability gates CycloneDX + VEX Public CVE advisories CSAF Vendor security bulletins CSAF FedRAMP compliance OSCAL POA&M tracking OSCAL License + vulnerability SPDX + VEX

// Set findings counts
report.Findings = pentest.FindingsSummary{
    Critical: 2,
    High:     5,
    Medium:   8,
    Low:      12,

        Severity:   "Critical",
        Status:     "In Progress",
        Owner:      "Platform Team",
        TargetDate: "2026-07-01",

docs.title: v0.21.0 Release Notes
docs.text: Release Date: August 22, 2026

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: This release introduces the residual risk model — vulnerability severity and risk before and after compensating controls, with exception-driven SLA switching — and titled vulnerability reports in Markdown, HTML, and PDF via the new reports/vulnreport package and govex report subcommand.

docs.title: Residual Risk Model
docs.text:
Vulnerabilities now carry their assessment before and after compensating controls, without relabeling the inherent severity:

  • CompensatingControl - Controls with function (preventive/detective/corrective), reduced risk dimensions, the CVSS environmental metrics they justify (ModifiedMetrics), effectiveness, and verification state
  • ExceptionStatus - Risk exception approval state with expiry
  • Residual fields - SeverityResidual, SeverityResidualVector, RiskInherent, RiskResidual, Controls, Exception
  • Effective severity - The SLA clock runs on inherent severity until an exception is approved, then on residual severity while the approval is in effect
  • Validation - Residual severity is restricted to Critical-Low and can never exceed the inherent severity
vn := govex.Vulnerability{
    Severity:         "High", // inherent: 30-day SLA
    SeverityResidual: "Low",  // residual: 180-day SLA
    Controls: []govex.CompensatingControl{{
        ID:              "CTRL-NET-001",
        Name:            "Network segmentation",
        Function:        govex.ControlFunctionPreventive,
        Reduces:         []string{govex.ReducesLikelihood},
        ModifiedMetrics: []string{"MAV:A"},
        Verified:        true,
    }},
    Exception: &govex.ExceptionStatus{
        Status:     govex.ExceptionStatusApproved,
        ApprovedAt: &approvedTime,
        ExpiresAt:  &expiryTime,
    },
}
sev := vn.EffectiveSeverity(time.Now()) // "Low" while approval is in effect

See Compensating Controls & Residual Risk.

docs.title: Risk Package
docs.text:
The new risk package models organization-level risk, distinct from CVSS-derived severity:

  • Rating - Likelihood × impact assessments with matrix reference, rationale, confidence, and assessor attribution
  • Matrix - Explicit likelihood × impact policy objects referenced by ID
  • NIST SP 800-30 - Level constants mapping 1:1 to the canonical scale (Very High↔Critical … Very Low↔Negligible), the standard's semi-quantitative 0-100 values, and translators for FedRAMP-style rendering

docs.title: Version-Specific CVSS Rating Scales
docs.text:
The cvss package aligns severity bands with the NVD qualitative ratings, per CVSS version:

  • CVSS v3.x and v4.0: None 0.0, Low 0.1-3.9, Medium 4.0-6.9, High 7.0-8.9, Critical 9.0-10.0
  • CVSS v2.0: no None or Critical; Low 0.0-3.9, High 7.0-10.0 — legacy v2 scores are never relabeled with v3/v4 bands

docs.title: Vulnerability Reports (vulnreport)
docs.text:
The new reports/vulnreport package renders a VulnerabilitiesSet as a titled report:

  • Metadata - Title, subtitle, organization, author, classification banner, period, executive summary
  • Sections - Severity summary table, findings table, and per-finding detail blocks with residual severity/risk and compensating controls
  • Formats - Markdown (GFM), standalone HTML (escaped, styled), PDF (maroto), and JSON round-trip
  • Columns - Default and residual-aware findings column sets, or custom column definitions

docs.title: govex report Subcommand
docs.text:
# HTML report from a vulnerabilities set JSON
govex report -i vulns.json -o report.html

# PDF with metadata and residual columns
govex report -i vulns.json -o report.pdf \
  --title "Q3 Vulnerability Report" \
  --classification "Confidential" \
  --columns residual

The input may be a VulnerabilitiesSet JSON (e.g. from govex merge) or a saved Report JSON; the output format is inferred from the file extension (.md, .html, .pdf, .json).

docs.title: Pentest Remediation Status Reports
docs.text: The reports/pentest package provides types and utilities for generating pentest remediation status letters that track penetration test findings, compensating controls, and remediation milestones.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Pentest remediation status reports help organizations communicate the progress of fixing security findings from penetration tests. These reports include:

  • Findings Summary - Counts by severity level
  • Remediation Status - Fixed vs. pending with completion percentage
  • Pending Items - Details on findings still being remediated
  • Compensating Controls - Mitigations in place for pending items
  • Milestones - Upcoming remediation phases

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
import "github.com/grokify/govex/reports/pentest"

// Create a new report
report := pentest.NewReport("Q2 2026 External Pentest Remediation Status")

// Set metadata
report.Metadata = pentest.Metadata{
    ReportName:     "External Network Penetration Test - Q2 2026",
    Assessor:       "SecureCo Consulting",
    AssessmentDate: "2026-04-15",
    ReportDate:     "2026-06-15",
    Author:         "Security Team",
    Scope:          "External-facing web applications and APIs",
}

// Set findings counts by severity
report.Findings = pentest.FindingsSummary{
    Critical: 2,
    High:     5,
    Medium:   8,
    Low:      12,
}

// Add pending items (findings still being remediated)
report.PendingItems = []pentest.PendingItem{
    {
        ID:               "PENTEST-001",
        Title:            "SQL Injection in Search API",
        Severity:         "Critical",
        Status:           "In Progress",
        Owner:            "Platform Team",
        TargetDate:       "2026-07-01",
        CompensatingCtrl: "CC-001",
    },
    {
        ID:             "PENTEST-003",
        Title:          "Missing Rate Limiting on Auth Endpoint",
        Severity:       "High",
        Status:         "Blocked",
        Owner:          "API Team",
        TargetDate:     "2026-07-15",
        BlockingReason: "Waiting for API gateway upgrade",
    },
}

// Add compensating controls
report.CompensatingControls = []pentest.CompensatingControl{
    {
        ID:             "CC-001",
        Title:          "WAF SQL Injection Rules",
        Description:    "ModSecurity rules deployed to block common SQL injection patterns.",
        FindingIDs:     []string{"PENTEST-001"},
        ImplementedOn:  "2026-04-20",
        EffectivenessS: "High - blocks 99% of known attack patterns",
    },
}

// Add milestones
report.NextMilestones = []pentest.Milestone{
    {
        Phase:       1,
        Title:       "Critical Findings Remediation",
        Description: "Fix all critical severity findings",
        TargetDate:  "2026-07-01",
        FindingIDs:  []string{"PENTEST-001", "PENTEST-002"},
        Owner:       "Platform Team",
    },
    {
        Phase:       2,
        Title:       "High Findings Remediation",
        Description: "Fix all high severity findings",
        TargetDate:  "2026-07-31",
        Owner:       "Security Team",
    },
}

// Calculate status from findings and pending items
report.CalculateStatus()

docs.title: Vulnerability Report (vulnreport)
docs.text: The reports/vulnreport package renders a VulnerabilitiesSet as a titled report in Markdown, HTML, and PDF, plus JSON for round-tripping. The VulnerabilitiesSet remains the data IR; vulnreport.Report adds report-level metadata and presentation.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: import "github.com/grokify/govex/reports/vulnreport"

docs.title: Report
docs.text:
r := vulnreport.NewReport("Q3 Vulnerability Report", set)
r.Subtitle = "Example App Security Assessment"
r.Organization = "Example Corp"
r.Author = "Security Team"
r.Classification = "Confidential" // rendered as a banner in HTML/PDF
r.GeneratedAt = &generatedTime
r.PeriodStart = &periodStart
r.PeriodEnd = &periodEnd
r.Summary = "Executive summary text. Blank lines separate paragraphs."

All metadata fields are optional; empty fields are omitted from the rendered header block. The header also includes the set's name, repository URL, data-as-of date, and finding count.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
md, err := r.Markdown()
html, err := r.HTML()
pdf, err := r.PDF() // []byte

err = r.WriteMarkdownFile("report.md", 0600)
err = r.WriteHTMLFile("report.html", 0600)
err = r.WritePDFFile("report.pdf", 0600)
err = r.WriteJSONFile("report.json", 0600)

Every format renders the same structure: classification banner, title, subtitle, metadata block, executive summary, severity summary table (counts ordered Critical to Low with a Total row), and the findings table.

After the findings table, HTML and Markdown output add a Finding Details section: one block per finding (an h3/### heading) with its name, ID, severity, inherent risk, description, and — when compensating controls exist — residual severity, residual risk, and each control's name and description in bold/italic emphasis (marked (verified) where applicable). Empty fields are omitted.

HTML output is a standalone page with inline styles; all cell values and metadata are HTML-escaped. Markdown output uses GitHub-flavored heading levels, tables, and bold/italic emphasis. PDF output uses maroto with page numbers and margins.

docs.title: Findings Columns
docs.text:
The findings table uses DefaultColumnDefinitionSet() unless Report.ColumnSet is set:

// Default: Severity, ID, Name, Category, Library, Library Version, Fixed Version
cols := vulnreport.DefaultColumnDefinitionSet()

// Residual-aware: ID, Name, Severity, Residual Severity, Residual Risk,
// Exception Status, Compensating Controls
cols = vulnreport.ResidualColumnDefinitionSet()
r.ColumnSet = &cols

ResidualColumnDefinitionSet renders the inherent vs. residual assessment model — see Compensating Controls & Residual Risk. The residual field names are also available for custom column sets:

cols := table.ColumnDefinitionSet{
    Definitions: []table.ColumnDefinition{
        {Name: govex.FieldID, SourceName: govex.FieldID},
        {Name: govex.FieldSeverity, SourceName: govex.FieldSeverity},
        {Name: govex.FieldSeverityResidual, SourceName: govex.FieldSeverityResidual},
        {Name: govex.FieldSeverityEffective, SourceName: govex.FieldSeverityEffective},
        {Name: govex.FieldRiskInherent, SourceName: govex.FieldRiskInherent},
        {Name: govex.FieldRiskResidual, SourceName: govex.FieldRiskResidual},
        {Name: govex.FieldExceptionStatus, SourceName: govex.FieldExceptionStatus},
        {Name: govex.FieldControls, SourceName: govex.FieldControls},
    },
}

FieldSeverityEffective evaluates the exception state at Vulnerability.ProcSLAEvalTime; set it before rendering time-sensitive reports.

PDF column limit

The PDF renderer distributes maroto's 12-cell grid across the table's columns, so a findings table may have at most 12 columns. Wider column sets return an error suggesting a narrower ColumnSet; Markdown and HTML have no such limit.

docs.title: CSAF Support
docs.text: Support for Common Security Advisory Framework (CSAF).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: import "github.com/grokify/govex/standards/csaf"

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: CSAF is an OASIS standard for machine-readable security advisories. It's the successor to CVRF (Common Vulnerability Reporting Framework) and is widely used by vendors for publishing security bulletins.

docs.title: When to Use CSAF
docs.text:
CSAF is best for:

  • Publishing security advisories to customers
  • Vendor CVE disclosure
  • Security bulletin automation
  • Threat intelligence feeds

For internal vulnerability triage, consider CycloneDX + VEX instead. See Vulnerability Formats for comparison.

docs.title: Parse CSAF Document
docs.text:
advisory, err := csaf.ParseFile("advisory.json")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

fmt.Println("Title:", advisory.Document.Title)
fmt.Println("Publisher:", advisory.Document.Publisher.Name)

docs.title: Convert to GoVEX
docs.text: vulns := advisory.ToVulnerabilities()

docs.title: CVSS Support
docs.text: Support for Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS).

docs.title: Installation

docs.title: Supported Versions
docs.text: Version Support CVSS 3.0 Full CVSS 3.1 Full CVSS 4.0 Partial

docs.title: Parse CVSS Vector
docs.text:
score, err := cvss30.ParseVector("CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

fmt.Println("Base Score:", score.BaseScore())
fmt.Println("Severity:", score.Severity())

docs.title: Calculate Score
docs.text:
// From vector components
score := cvss30.Score{
    AttackVector:       "Network",
    AttackComplexity:   "Low",
    PrivilegesRequired: "None",
    UserInteraction:    "None",
    Scope:              "Unchanged",
    Confidentiality:    "High",
    Integrity:          "High",
    Availability:       "High",
}

base := score.Calculate()

docs.title: Qualitative Severity Rating Scales
docs.text:
GoVEX aligns with the NVD qualitative severity ratings. The rating bands are version-specific and provided by the cvss package:

import "github.com/grokify/govex/cvss"

set, err := cvss.SeveritySetForVersion("3.1") // accepts "2.0", "3.0", "3.1", "3.x", "4.0"
sev, err := set.SeverityFromScoreFloat32(3.9) // "Low"

docs.title: CVSS v3.x and v4.0
docs.text:
CVSS v3.0, v3.1, and v4.0 share the same rating bands:

Score Range Rating 0.0 None 0.1 - 3.9 Low 4.0 - 6.9 Medium 7.0 - 8.9 High 9.0 - 10.0 Critical

docs.title: CVSS v2.0
docs.text:
CVSS v2.0 defines no None or Critical rating; Low starts at 0.0 and High extends to 10.0:

Score Range Rating 0.0 - 3.9 Low 4.0 - 6.9 Medium 7.0 - 10.0 High

Do not relabel v2 scores with v3/v4 bands

A CVSS v2.0 score of 9.8 is High under the v2 scale. It must not be relabeled Critical unless re-derived from a v3.x or v4.0 vector. Use cvss.SeveritySetCVSS2() for legacy v2-scored data.

docs.title: Base vs. Environmental Severity
docs.text: The base score yields the inherent severity. A CVSS environmental score — the base metrics modified by verified compensating controls (e.g. MAV:A for network segmentation) — yields the residual severity, using the same rating bands. See Compensating Controls & Residual Risk.

docs.title: Vector String Format
docs.text:
CVSS 3.1 vector format:

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
Metric Values AV (Attack Vector) N (Network), A (Adjacent), L (Local), P (Physical) AC (Attack Complexity) L (Low), H (High) PR (Privileges Required) N (None), L (Low), H (High) UI (User Interaction) N (None), R (Required) S (Scope) U (Unchanged), C (Changed) C (Confidentiality) N (None), L (Low), H (High) I (Integrity) N (None), L (Low), H (High) A (Availability) N (None), L (Low), H (High)
